name: Mai Brat
confidence_why: Dol 1999/2007 calls Maybrat stress weakly phonemic and only "as a rule" initial, listing doublets and unpredictable non-initial forms, and Brown 1991 finds phonemic stress on any syllable with minimal pairs, so initial stress is the clear default but the fixed: initial syllable coding overstates both first-hand descriptions.
catalog_quote: Lexical Stress in Maybrat seems to be weakly phonemic, as it cannot be fully predicted. However, some generalisations which predict stress can be made: stress can only fall on a phonemic, non-reduced V. As a rule, main stress ... falls on the initial syllable of bisyllabic words ... and most trisyllabic words... In trisyllabic words, a secondary stress ... may be heard on the final syllable. (Dol…

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (initial main stress as the default in simplex 2-3 syllable words, window 2-3, optional final secondary in trisyllables; lexical exceptions/doublets), i.e. drop from the strict set and drop the projected n>=4 alternating rows; add caution 'Brown 1991 (Ayamaru dialect): stress phonemic, any syllable'.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: The quotation is genuine and the source behind it (Dol 1999/2007) is the best description of Maybrat stress and is held, so sourcing per se is sound. The problem is the classification drawn from it. 'fixed-strict' with alternating stress from the left overstates Dol on three counts visible on pp.38-40 of the held grammar: (i) Dol calls stress 'weakly phonemic.. cannot be fully predicted', lists stress doublets (ex.46 kapan ~ kaˈpan etc.) and forms with unpredictable non-initial stress (ex.47 paˈyir, oˈra, aˈfi, aˈyo), and says (fn.36) misplaced stress is corrected by speakers; (ii) schwa-initial /CəCi-jV/ trisyllables take FINAL main stress (ex.43 fəniˈja 'woman'); (iii) words of four or more syllables are compounds whose main stress sits on the second member with secondaries radiating from it (ex.45 ˌpɔrˈmapuˌwo, main on syllable 2), so the coded 1010/10101/.. rows have no support — a point our ow

sources.citation: Brown, William U. 1991. A quantitative phonology of Mai Brat. In Tom Dutton (ed.), Papers in Papuan linguistics No. 1, 1-27. Pacific Linguistics A-73. Canberra: ANU. (CC BY-SA online edition, sealang.net/CRCL)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'The phonological word ... in Mai Brat is the domain of one stress. A word may consist of one to four phonetic syllables. Two-syllable words predominate [Table 1: 69.2% of 1,911 lexemes disyllabic, 1.4% four syllables] ... Stress is phonemic and can occur on any syllable of the word.' with minimal pairs /'nasom/ 'you carry' vs /na'som/ 'your name is', /'maru/ 'she cuts' vs /ma'ru/ 'lake', /'ana/ 'they' vs /a'na/ 'fence', /'moo/ 'she takes' vs /mo'o/ 'she itches'; p.26: 'Most stress pairs in Mai Brat are differentiated by semantic context.'
sources.locator: p.2, section 2 'Stress and the phonological word' (Kambuaya village, Ayamaru dialect)
sources.note: The only other phonological description (Ayamaru dialect); states stress is phonemic on any syllable with minimal pairs, directly against a 'fixed-strict' coding; Dol 2007 fn.20 cites and disputes it. Listed as 'unfetched' in our first check; now obtained.
